title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
content: US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August. Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher petrol prices, which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The elections are being fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US. Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%. Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI). It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy. The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change. There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise. If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example. Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices. Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel. Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100. Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices. Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months. In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year. Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%. Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027. The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month. The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December. Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world. While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost. In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax. Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas. Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year. While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years. During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up. Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel. Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%. It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace. A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates. Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions. Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand. The rate of UK economic growth affects things like pay increases and the amount of tax raised. With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves. US inflation continues to rise, and this month the jump was above forecasts. Here's how some are surviving. With the ongoing war in the Middle East increasing prices, one deputy is ask for duty to be frozen. On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised UK plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: 'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
content: Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years. The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything". She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise . Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers for September that were released on Wednesday. The price rise was more than economists and Wall Street analysts had forecast. High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans. Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family. "I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark." Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money. And it is still not enough to support her family. Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home. "I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said. The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult. And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline. "I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (£4.5)," he said. Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control." He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up. The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, the index was -40. In May, it reached -45, the lowest since 2022. A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis. This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that. When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef." As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said. Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken. "[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said. Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month. "I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically." For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming. She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies. Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice. The family has even decided to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much. "It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot." Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived. The Since U Been Gone singer claims she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" an item in the store. Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US. Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated. The school has faced an uproar over how it handled assault allegations brought by a woman known as Jane Doe. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
content: The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey. Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction. It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week. Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time. Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will". But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending". The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August. "It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said. The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain". Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply. The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted. Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period. But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period. August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%. Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought". He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs". PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance. "The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added. Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register". He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents. The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations. Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks." The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget". Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing." He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate". "The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet." The influential economics body has upgraded its UK growth forecast for this year, but risks remain. The prediction from the IMF comes as final preparations are being made for the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
